1721.t: From διαβάλλω (diabállō, “to slander”, from δια- (dia-, “through”) + βάλλω (bállō, “to throw”)). For the meaning development, compare Russian кида́ла (kidála), кида́лово (kidálovo) related to кида́ть (kidátʹ).

1773.t: Etymology tree Ancient Greek μυέω (mŭéō) Proto-Indo-European *-tósder.

1761.t: From Phoenician 𐤑𐤉𐤃𐤅𐤍 (ṣydwn /⁠Ṣīdūn⁠/). Cognate with Hebrew צִידוֹן (Ṣīḏōn) and Aramaic ܨܝܕܘܢ (Ṣidon).

1738.t: From πίπτω (pī́ptō, “to fall”) + -μα (-mă, resultative noun suffix). (corpse): Compare typologically Latin cadāver (< cadō), Russian па́даль (pádalʹ) (akin to па́дать (pádatʹ)).

1759.t: The feminine substantive form of the adjective μεσοποτάμιος (mesopotámios) from μεσο- (meso-, “middle, between”) + ποταμός (potamós, “river”), compare with the Hebrew אֲרַם נַהֲרַיִם.

1740.t: From συν- (sŭn-, “with”) + the root of γίγνομαι (gígnomai, “to be born”) + -ής (-ḗs, adjectival suffix).

1730.t: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- Proto-Indo-European *-yeti Proto-Indo-European *(s)kéryeti Proto-Hellenic *keřřō Ancient Greek κείρω From Proto-Hellenic *keřřō, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kér-ye-, *ye-present from the root *(s)ker- (“to cut”).

1791.t: From Proto-Indo-European *bʰol-yom, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰleh₃- (“leaf, blossom, flower”). Cognates include Latin folium, Old Armenian բողբոջ (bołboǰ), and English blossom.

1760.t: Old Iranian name, from Old Persian 𐎶𐎠𐎭 (m-a-d /⁠Māda-⁠/), but of uncertain meaning; possibly from Proto-Iranian *mádyah (“in the middle”). Folk etymology connected it to Μήδεια (Mḗdeia), granddaughter of Helios.

1709.t: From ἐπι- (epĭ-, “upon”) + φαίνω (phaínō, “to shine, bring to light”).

1776.t: From Proto-Hellenic *nid͏̌d͏̌ō, from Proto-Indo-European *nigʷ-ye-, from *neygʷ- (“to wash”). Compare Proto-Germanic *nikwes, Old English nicor, German Nix.

1775.t: From Proto-Hellenic *nā́us, from Proto-Indo-European *néh₂us (“boat”), cognate with Latin nāvis, Persian ناو (nâv), and Sanskrit नौ (nau, “ship”), नाव (nāva, “ship”).

1742.t: From Proto-Hellenic *tʰrépʰō with deaspiration of the /tʰ/ to /t/ by Grassmann's law everywhere except in forms where the /pʰ/ has been deaspirated to /p/ by a following consonant (future, first aorist, perfect middle).

1718.t: This word and the synonymous βόθυνος (bóthunos) have been connected with Latin fodiō (“to dig”), Lithuanian bedù (“sting, dig”) and Middle Welsh beð (“canal”), assuming either a dissimilation of Proto-Indo-European *bʰodʰ- to Proto-Hellenic *bodʰ-, which…

1734.t: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *leb- Proto-Indo-European *-os Proto-Indo-European *-ós Proto-Indo-European *-ós Proto-Indo-European *lobós Proto-Hellenic *lobós? Ancient Greek λοβός Uncertain, though perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *leb- (“to hang…

1798.t: From ἀνα- (ana-, “on, up”) + ἅπτω (háptō, “touch, fasten, ignite”).

1731.t: From Proto-Indo-European *ḱéytor, from *ḱey- (“to lie down”). Cognate with Latin cūnae, cīvis, Old Armenian սէր (sēr), Hittite 𒆠𒀉𒋫𒊑, 𒆠𒀉𒁕𒊑 (kittari), Sanskrit शेते (śéte).

1713.t: From the stem of ἡμεῖς (hēmeîs, “we”) + -τερος (-teros, contrastive suffix).

1765.t: From Proto-Hellenic *dótis, from Proto-Indo-European *déh₃tis. By surface analysis, δίδωμι (dídōmi, “to give”) + -σις (-sis, verbal noun suffix).

1706.t: From ἐκ (ek, “out”), formed on the model of ἐντός (entós, “within, inside”). Cognate with Old Irish acht (“but, provided that”), Gothic 𐌰𐌹𐌸𐌸𐌰𐌿 (aiþþau, “or, otherwise”).

1768.t: Perhaps from Proto-Hellenic *lantʰánō, from Proto-Indo-European *lh₂-n-dʰ-, nasal infix present of *leh₂-dʰ-, dental extension of *leh₂- (“to be hidden, be covered”).

1790.t: Traditionally regarded as a formation from τύπτω (tŭ́ptō, “to strike, beat, smite”) + -ανον (-ănon), similar to that of ὄργανον (órganon, “instrument, sense organ”).

1715.t: From Proto-Hellenic *óletʰros, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃elh₁dʰros, from *h₃elh₁- (“to destroy”). Cognate with ὄλλυμι (óllūmĭ).

1711.t: From ἑκατόν (hekatón, “hundred”) + ἀρχός (arkhós, “ruler”). Calque of Old Persian *θatapatiš (“commander of a hundred men”).

1722.t: Traditionally derived from a u-stem formation of δικεῖν (dikeîn, “to throw”).

1786.t: From Proto-Indo-European *spend-. Cognate to Latin spondeo.

1700.t: From ἀνατίθημι (anatíthēmi, “to dedicate”) and the suffix -μα (-ma).

1732.t: Borrowed from Biblical Hebrew כִּנּוֹר (kinnōr) and adapted to κινυρός (kinurós, “wailing”).

1739.t: This word is usually derived from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂ǵ- (“to attach”) (given by Beekes as *ph₂k- (“stiff, hard”)).

1733.t: Often connected to κλείς (kleís, “key”). Alternatively, the word could be Pre-Greek.

1784.t: Connection with ψίομαι (psíomai, “to chew”) is semantically attractive, but the formation is quite unclear. Since an Indo-European origin is formally hardly possible, the word could well be Pre-Greek.

1769.t: Unexplained. Perhaps a technical term of the Pre-Greek substrate.

1712.t: Probably from ἕδος (hédos, “seat”) + a suffix -(α)φος (-(a)phos), though Beekes expresses some doubt, perhaps due to the strange morphology of the suffix.

1701.t: Perhaps from a Proto-Indo-European *h₂pelH- (“to speak publicly”), and related via this root to Latvian pel̂t (“to revile”).

1704.t: From ἀμάω (amáō, “to harvest, gather”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂meh₁- (“to reap, mow, harvest”) (whence also English mow, meadow).

1783.t: πῦρ (pûr, “fire”) + -εῖον (-eîon, suffix forming nouns denoting instruments or toponyms)
